questions.text: Who pushes on what: receptors, messengers and the inotropes

steps.bridge: Three of these four drugs work through cyclic AMP. Your grand tests asked what it does inside the cell. Open the cell.

lesson.text:
Begin with the pump, the number that failed in Patient A. Four drugs on this card push on it, and it carries more bank questions than any other card in the packet. One idea holds all four.

A heart muscle cell contracts when calcium meets its filaments. So there are only two ways to make it contract harder. Give the filaments more calcium, or make them more sensitive to the calcium they have. Three of these drugs take the first road, through one messenger, cyclic AMP. The fourth takes the second.

Dobutamine. It stimulates the beta-one receptor, cyclic AMP rises, and with it the contractility and the heart rate. It also stimulates beta-two receptors on the arterioles, which dilate. More pump, less squeeze: the card calls it inodilation. Two things follow, and both are asked. The tachycardia isn't a reflex. It's the direct beta-one effect, it climbs with the dose, and it's the toxic effect the banks key. And because dobutamine dilates, the pressure can fall on it.

Epinephrine. Beta-one again, and at higher doses alpha-one, so the vessels constrict. It also raises the lactate, through beta-two receptors driving glycolysis. That lactate isn't hypoperfusion, so it can mislead you. In infarct shock, the small OptimaCC trial found more refractory shock with epinephrine than with norepinephrine.

Milrinone works one step further in. Cyclic AMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase three. Block that enzyme, and cyclic AMP builds up with no receptor touched. In the heart, more contraction. In the vessels, dilation, most of all in the pulmonary vessels. Its main unwanted effect is hypotension, which is vasodilation and not toxicity. And the kidney clears it, so in renal failure you lower the rate and leave out the loading dose.

Levosimendan takes the other road. It binds troponin C and makes it more sensitive to calcium. No extra calcium enters the cell, so in theory it costs less oxygen and provokes fewer arrhythmias. It also opens potassium channels in the vessel wall, so the afterload falls. And an active metabolite keeps it working for days.

{{**Drug** | **Acts at** | **Net**
Dobutamine | β1 + β2 | inodilator; direct tachycardia
Epinephrine | β1; α1 at high dose | lactate ↑ (β2)
Milrinone | PDE-3 block → cAMP ↑ | pulmonary dilation; renal clearance
Levosimendan | troponin C + K-ATP | no Ca²⁺ rise; lasts days}}

Now see what all four share. [[Every inotrope on this card also dilates vessels. So when the pressure falls on an inotrope, the answer is to add norepinephrine, not to cut the inotrope and not to change to milrinone.]]

That's where the trap forms. A patient on dobutamine, heart rate one hundred and thirty, still hypotensive. One bank key says decrease the dobutamine. That key is disputed, because less dobutamine does nothing for the pressure. So read the stem. If it stresses the low pressure, add norepinephrine. If it stresses a tachyarrhythmia with an adequate pressure, reduce the dose. And if the patient is on high-dose norepinephrine with a low output, add dobutamine.

One newer name, asked by two banks. Omecamtiv mecarbil is a cardiac myosin activator. It lengthens ejection, so the stroke volume rises with no rise in cyclic AMP, calcium or oxygen use. The distractor beside it is serelaxin, a vasodilator and not an inotrope.

[[Dobutamine and epinephrine raise cyclic AMP at the receptor. Milrinone raises it by blocking its breakdown. Levosimendan raises the sensitivity to calcium instead.]]

But what does cyclic AMP do inside the cell? Your grand tests asked exactly that, three times.

steps.bridge: α1 has brought you from the pump to the squeeze. When the squeeze fails, which drug comes first, and in what order?

lesson.text:
Three of your grand test questions sit inside one heart cell, and you missed two of them. They're the same pathway, asked at three points. Walk it once, slowly.

The beta-one receptor is coupled to a G protein called Gs, s for stimulatory. When dobutamine binds, Gs switches on adenylate cyclase, which makes cyclic AMP. Cyclic AMP switches on one enzyme, protein kinase A. Everything after that is protein kinase A adding a phosphate to a target. There are four targets, and they do two jobs.

The first job is to contract harder. Protein kinase A phosphorylates the L-type calcium channel in the membrane, so more calcium enters with each beat. And it phosphorylates the ryanodine receptor, the release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so more of the store is released. More calcium in systole. That's inotropy.

The second job is to relax faster. After each beat, calcium is pumped back into the store by a pump called SERCA, which works with a brake on it, a small protein called phospholamban. Protein kinase A phosphorylates phospholamban, the brake comes off, and calcium is cleared faster. It also phosphorylates troponin I, so the filaments let go of calcium sooner. That's lusitropy.

[[Protein kinase A phosphorylates the L-type channel and the ryanodine receptor for contraction, and phospholamban for relaxation. All of it lies downstream of beta-one, Gs and cyclic AMP.]]

{{**β1** → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → **PKA**
Inotropy: L-type Ca²⁺ channel, **ryanodine receptor**
Lusitropy: **phospholamban** (frees SERCA2a), troponin I
**α1** → Gq → **phospholipase C** → IP3 (Ca²⁺ release) + DAG (PKC)}}

Now the two you got wrong. How does beta-one stimulation improve relaxation? You chose myosin ATPase. The key is phosphorylation of phospholamban. How does dobutamine improve contraction? You chose inhibition of myosin kinase. The key is phosphorylation of the ryanodine receptor. Both wrong options put the action on myosin. In the heart cell, the answers are about handling calcium. Inhibition of myosin light chain kinase is real, but it belongs to smooth muscle. It's how beta-two relaxes a vessel.

Now cross to that vessel. The alpha-one receptor is coupled to a different G protein, Gq. Gq switches on phospholipase C, which splits a membrane lipid into two messengers. Inositol trisphosphate, IP three, releases calcium from the store. Diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C. Calcium rises, and the vessel constricts. So when a stem asks how norepinephrine raises the pressure, the key is phospholipase C. The wrong option is cyclic AMP, the beta arm.

[[Beta receptors use Gs and cyclic AMP. Alpha-one uses Gq and phospholipase C, giving IP three and diacylglycerol.]]

One drug closes the cell. Isoproterenol, or isoprenaline, is pure beta, with no alpha. Beta-one drives the rate and contractility up, so the oxygen demand rises. Beta-two opens the vessels, so the diastolic pressure falls, and the coronaries fill in diastole. Demand up, supply down. The harm the exam keys is myocardial ischaemia, which is why in shock it's used mainly as a bridge to pacing in bradycardia.

And alpha-one has just carried you across to the squeeze.

steps.bridge: In sepsis the ladder says no to levosimendan. Yet twice your grand tests wanted it. The patient was on a β-blocker.

lesson.text:
Now the squeeze. Go back to Patient B, warm, her vessels wide open. Her failed number is the SVR, and this card is the order in which you restore it. You met this ladder in your viva package. Here it is for the MCQ, with eleven bank questions on it.

First line is norepinephrine, the only drug on the ladder with a strong recommendation to give it. You can now say how it works. Alpha-one, through Gq, restores the squeeze, and a modest beta-one effect holds the output up.

Why not dopamine? One trial, SOAP two. One thousand six hundred and seventy-nine patients in shock, dopamine against norepinephrine. NEET's favourite wrong option is that norepinephrine improved survival. It didn't.

[[SOAP two: dopamine and norepinephrine had the same mortality at twenty-eight days, but dopamine gave twice the arrhythmias, twenty-four percent against twelve, and more deaths in the cardiogenic subgroup.]]

So dopamine is left for highly selected patients, with a low risk of tachyarrhythmia or with bradycardia. And low-dose dopamine to protect the kidney is recommended against.

The second rung. When the norepinephrine dose is climbing, add vasopressin. Added, not swapped. It works through its own receptor, V one, which acidosis and a flood of catecholamines haven't worn down. And septic shock brings a relative lack of vasopressin.

The third rung. If the mean pressure is still inadequate, add epinephrine.

Then the branch back to the pump. Filling adequate, pressure adequate, and the patient still hypoperfused. That's a heart weakened by sepsis. Add dobutamine to the norepinephrine, or use epinephrine alone. The banks make this a false-statement question, and the false statement is to avoid dobutamine.

The discouraged list: terlipressin, levosimendan, and low-dose dopamine for the kidney.

{{**Septic shock ladder**
1 Norepinephrine (**strong**)
2 + Vasopressin on escalating dose
3 + Epinephrine
Cardiac dysfunction: + dobutamine, or epinephrine alone
Against: terlipressin, levosimendan, renal-dose dopamine
Wean: norepinephrine first, vasopressin last}}

One more question is about coming down. The pressure holds, the lactate is falling, and the patient is on norepinephrine and vasopressin. Which do you taper first? Norepinephrine. In retrospective studies, stopping vasopressin first caused more hypotension. In the same stem, the antibiotics are narrowed by the cultures, not run for a fixed fourteen days.

[[Up the ladder: norepinephrine, then add vasopressin, then add epinephrine, with dobutamine when the heart is the problem. Down the ladder: norepinephrine comes off first.]]

Why is a sepsis card in a cardiology packet? Because the same rung comes first in cardiogenic shock. When Patient A needs a pressor, it's norepinephrine.

Now notice one word on the discouraged list. Levosimendan.

steps.bridge: One card left on the squeeze: what to do when norepinephrine causes harm, or when it simply isn't enough.

lesson.text:
In sepsis the guideline suggests against levosimendan. Yet in two different grand tests the key was levosimendan, and you chose epinephrine. What changed? The stem said the patient was on a chronic beta-blocker.

Go back into the cell. The pathway begins at the beta-one receptor, and a beta-blocker sits on it. So any drug that starts there, dobutamine or epinephrine, has to compete, and its effect is blunted.

Epinephrine has a second problem. Its beta effects are blocked, but its alpha-one effect isn't. So you get vasoconstriction without inotropy, and the afterload rises on a failing ventricle. That makes it the wrong option, not merely the weaker one.

So go past the receptor. Milrinone blocks phosphodiesterase three, so cyclic AMP rises with no receptor involved. Levosimendan doesn't need cyclic AMP at all. It acts on troponin C, at the filament.

[[In a patient on a chronic beta-blocker, beta-agonists are blunted. Choose a drug that acts beyond the receptor: levosimendan, or milrinone.]]

Which of the two? Your grand tests keyed levosimendan both times, so choose it when it's offered. If only milrinone is offered, choose milrinone. NEET in twenty twenty-four asked about milrinone from the other side, and the fact it turned on was that milrinone works downstream of the beta receptor. The European heart failure guideline says the same: levosimendan or a phosphodiesterase three inhibitor may be considered to reverse the effect of a beta-blocker.

Both dilate, so keep norepinephrine ready.

So one drug is discouraged in one stem and keyed in another. In sepsis, with nothing on the receptor, it adds nothing. On a beta-blocker, it's the drug that still works.

steps.bridge: You know what each drug pushes on. Now the order: what you give first, and to which patient.

lesson.text:
Back to the squeeze, for the edges of the ladder. Three situations, each answered by the receptor or pathway the drug uses.

First. A patient in septic shock on norepinephrine develops a tachyarrhythmia. That's its beta-one effect. You still need the squeeze, so you want alpha-one with nothing else: phenylephrine. It holds the tone without stimulating the heart. Its price is on the pump, because it raises the afterload with no inotropy, so it's a drug for this situation and not first line. The bank asked it as a stroke patient with a low mean pressure and fast atrial fibrillation, and fewer than a third chose it.

Second, a number. Vasopressin is added when norepinephrine reaches zero point two five to zero point five micrograms per kilogram per minute.

Third. High-dose norepinephrine after a liver transplant or bypass, and the vessels still won't constrict. That's vasoplegia, and it runs on another messenger. Nitric oxide switches on soluble guanylate cyclase, which makes cyclic GMP, which relaxes smooth muscle. Methylene blue blocks that chain twice.

[[Methylene blue raises vascular tone by inhibiting nitric oxide synthase and soluble guanylate cyclase. It has no action on adrenergic receptors.]]

Only seven percent of candidates picked that statement.

There are four rescue agents for vasoplegia. Vasopressin. Angiotensin two, from the ATHOS three trial. Methylene blue. And hydroxocobalamin, which mops up nitric oxide. The trap is a fifth name. Angiotensin one is an inactive precursor that needs converting enzyme in the lung. It's the least likely to raise the pressure, and only one in six got that right.

{{**Tachyarrhythmia on norepinephrine** → phenylephrine (pure α1)
**Add vasopressin** at norepinephrine 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min
**Vasoplegia rescue:** vasopressin, angiotensin II, methylene blue, hydroxocobalamin
**Not a drug:** angiotensin I}}

That's the pharmacy. Beta-one and what lies beyond it for the pump. Alpha-one, V one and nitric oxide for the squeeze. Next comes the harder skill, which is order.

spine: Contract harder = more calcium at the filament, or more sensitivity to it. Dobutamine, epinephrine and milrinone raise cAMP; levosimendan sensitises troponin C.
β1 → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → PKA: L-type channel + ryanodine receptor (inotropy), phospholamban + troponin I (lusitropy).
α1 → Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 + DAG → vasoconstriction. Isoproterenol (pure β): rate up, diastolic pressure down → myocardial ischaemia.
Every inotrope also vasodilates: if the pressure falls on an inotrope, add norepinephrine. Squeeze ladder: norepinephrine → + vasopressin → + epinephrine.
Chronic β-blocker: β-agonists are blunted. Go past the receptor: levosimendan (keyed) or milrinone.
Tachyarrhythmia on norepinephrine → phenylephrine. Vasoplegia rescue: vasopressin, angiotensin II, methylene blue (blocks NOS and sGC), hydroxocobalamin.

open.text:
Go back to Patient A. Anterior infarct, cold and wet, a pressure of eighty-two over fifty. In Shock One you learned to read him. His pump has failed, his squeeze has clamped down to hold the pressure up, and his filling is backing up into his lungs.

Now you have to do something. And here's the uncomfortable truth about every drug you're about to meet. Each one pushes on one of the three numbers, and each push sends the injured heart a bill, paid in oxygen.

Push the pump with an inotrope, and the heart beats harder and faster, and needs more oxygen to do it. Push the squeeze with a vasopressor, and the pressure rises, but the ventricle now pumps against a higher wall. Take away filling with a diuretic, and the lungs clear, but only if the heart was over-filled to begin with.

[[Every drug and every device pushes on one of the three numbers. The best treatment pushes where the failure is, and sends the heart the smallest bill.]]

So the packet runs in the order you'd think at the bedside. First, the drugs, and the receptors they act through, because NEET asks the receptors directly. Then the ladder: what you do first, second and third. Then the special cases, where a valve or a hole in the septum changes the rules. Then the treatment with the strongest proof of saving lives, opening the artery. And last, the machines, for when drugs are not enough.

Five of the questions in this packet were misses in your grand tests, and one of them you missed twice. Listen for them.

Start with the pump. How does a drug make a heart muscle cell contract harder?

questions.text: The ladder of treatment: offload first, then push

steps.bridge: The right place, the right team. Now what that team aims at: five targets, which are your three numbers again.

lesson.text:
Before any drug, a place. This card hasn't been asked directly, so take it quickly.

Three things earn an intensive care bed: pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, and heart failure appearing for the first time. When chronic heart failure suddenly decompensates, look for the trigger: an infection, anaemia or renal dysfunction.

One line could become an MCQ. [[The European guideline holds that a cardiac intensive care unit is better than a general one. The American heart association advocates neither.]]

And volume matters. Centres treating more than about a hundred cases a year have a lower in-hospital mortality. So the patient bypasses the nearest hospital and goes straight to a hub with a shock team.

steps.bridge: Five targets on paper. At the bedside you choose among them with two questions: warm or cold, wet or dry.

lesson.text:
What does that team aim at? Five targets: your three numbers, with rate and rhythm added.

Rate and rhythm first, and the aim is normal sinus rhythm. Too fast and the ventricle can't fill. Too slow and the output falls.

Preload. In the wet patient you lower it, with diuretics, or renal replacement if they fail. Won't that drop the output? Hardly. The failing ventricle sits on the flat part of its curve, the one you used in Shock One. There, less filling relieves the lungs and costs almost no stroke volume.

Afterload. You lower it with a vasodilator such as nitroglycerin. A failing ventricle is very sensitive to afterload, so a small fall in resistance gives a large rise in stroke volume.

And contraction: the inotropes, with norepinephrine alongside, because the pressure can fall on them.

[[A vasodilator and an inotrope both raise the stroke volume. The vasodilator does it without raising oxygen demand. The inotrope does it at the cost of more demand and more arrhythmia.]]

That's the reason for the order.

steps.bridge: Offloading has three tools. Start with the one that isn't a drug at all: positive pressure.

lesson.text:
You met the four boxes in Shock One: warm or cold for the pump, wet or dry for the filling. You met this algorithm in your viva package. Now each box gets its treatment. Nine bank questions sit here, and three of the bank keys need care. First the logic, then the stems.

A sense of proportion. Ninety-five percent of patients with acute heart failure are wet, and five percent are dry. So the real decision is about perfusion.

Wet and warm: congested but perfusing. Offloading is all he needs. If a high blood pressure dominates, the vascular type, the fluid hasn't been gained. It's been pushed into the lungs by a sudden rise in afterload, so the vasodilator leads. If congestion dominates, the cardiac type, fluid has been gained over days, so the diuretic leads, with ultrafiltration if it fails.

Wet and cold is the danger, and the card cuts it at a systolic of ninety. Below ninety, perfusion comes first: an inotrope, a vasopressor if refractory, mechanical support if drugs fail, and the diuretic only once perfusion is corrected. Why wait? A diuretic lowers the filling of a heart that's already failing to deliver flow. At ninety or above you can offload, with vasodilators and diuretics.

Dry and warm is compensated: adjust the oral drugs. Dry and cold is hypoperfused and empty: a fluid challenge, then an inotrope if needed.

[[Wet with a pressure gets a diuretic and a vasodilator. Wet and cold below ninety gets perfusion first and the diuretic later. Dry and cold gets fluid.]]

Now the stems.

Congestion with a pressure of ninety-five over sixty. The tempting answer is norepinephrine. But ninety-five is above ninety, and perfusion isn't failing. That's wet and warm: intravenous furosemide.

Reduced ejection fraction, eighty-five over fifty, heart rate one hundred and twenty. One bank keys dobutamine, following this European algorithm. The American statements start norepinephrine at that pressure. So use the wording. If the stem says low output and asks for an inotrope, choose dobutamine. If it says shock with a mean pressure under sixty-five and offers norepinephrine, choose norepinephrine.

A patient who was one hundred and twenty over eighty becomes hypotensive after diuresis. One key says dopamine, and it's outdated. This is over-diuresis. Hold the diuretic and reassess the volume. Milrinone would only dilate him further.

{{**Stem** | **Exam answer**
Wet, SBP ≥90 (even 95/60) | IV loop diuretic
Wet, hypertensive (SBP 180+) | Nitroglycerin, NIV, then furosemide
Low output, SBP 85, asks for an inotrope | Dobutamine
Shock, MAP <65, norepinephrine offered | Norepinephrine, then dobutamine
Hypotension after diuresis | Stop the diuretic, reassess volume}}

Hypertensive pulmonary oedema, first-line reducer of preload: nitroglycerin. Nitroprusside needs an arterial line and carries cyanide, so it's kept for refractory hypertension and acute valve regurgitation.

One mimic. Flash pulmonary oedema that keeps returning, with resistant hypertension and a rising creatinine, is bilateral renal artery stenosis, Pickering syndrome. Renal angiography with stenting prevents it. Renal denervation doesn't.

[[Dopamine is no longer the first choice in cardiogenic shock. And hypotension that appears after diuresis is over-diuresis: stop the diuretic before reaching for any drug.]]

So most patients are wet with a pressure, and for them the treatment is offloading.

steps.bridge: Positive pressure offloads in seconds. Two drugs do the same job, and the stem's blood pressure tells you which leads.

lesson.text:
One line on this card is a treatment in its own right, and it's the line the examiners test. Positive pressure ventilation has a positive effect on left ventricular function. Why should a ventilator help a heart?

Think about what the ventricle pushes against. Its wall has to generate the difference between the pressure inside the cavity and the pressure around the heart. That's the transmural pressure. Raise the pressure in the chest, and for the same aortic pressure the wall has less to generate. That's a fall in afterload, with no drug given. The raised pressure also reduces venous return, so the preload falls too.

The right ventricle sees it differently, and NEET asked this in twenty twenty-four.

[[Positive end-expiratory pressure lowers right ventricular preload, raises right ventricular afterload, and lowers left ventricular afterload.]]

The trap: the statement that CPAP mainly reduces preload is keyed false, because it lowers afterload as well. And it does so by raising intrathoracic pressure, not by lowering alveolar pressure and not through renin.

Run it backwards. Remove the positive pressure at a spontaneous breathing trial, and preload and afterload return at once. That's weaning-induced pulmonary oedema.

So for the alert patient with a systolic of one hundred and eighty and pink frothy sputum, the answer is nitrates with non-invasive ventilation, not a diuretic alone and not immediate intubation.

If you must intubate, the card prefers etomidate, which disturbs the circulation least. Its price is the adrenal gland. One grand test gave a patient on phenytoin and ketoconazole who received etomidate and developed shock that answered to hydrocortisone. Which drug was responsible? All of them. Fewer than half chose that.

Three numbers. Ventilate at six millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight. About twenty percent of patients in cardiogenic shock need continuous renal replacement. And it's considered from KDIGO stage two.

steps.bridge: When offloading is not enough, the pump itself must be pushed. That needs an algorithm, and it has one branch.

lesson.text:
Now the offloading drugs, and the bank asks about one patient: the one whose lungs flood in minutes with a very high pressure.

The loop diuretic lowers the circulating volume, but that takes hours. The card adds that it's a mild venodilator, and that effect comes within minutes. Nitroglycerin dilates veins and arteries. At low doses the veins dominate and the preload falls. At high doses the arteries open too, and the afterload falls. Non-invasive ventilation lowers left ventricular wall stress. And dialysis removes volume and corrects electrolytes.

Now the patient. A surge of sympathetic tone clamps the vessels, the afterload jumps, and the left ventricle can't eject against it. Blood backs up into the lungs. He hasn't gained fluid. It has been redistributed. This is sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema, SCAPE. So a diuretic alone is too slow, and it does nothing for the afterload.

[[In hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema, high-dose intravenous nitrate with non-invasive ventilation comes first. Furosemide comes second. Morphine is no longer routine.]]

NEET asked it two years running. In twenty twenty-five, pulmonary oedema with a pressure of one hundred and eighty over one hundred: nitroglycerin with furosemide. In twenty twenty-four, the same after bypass surgery: nitroglycerin.

The discriminator is the history. Days of weight gain with a normal pressure means fluid gained, and the diuretic leads. Sudden onset with a high pressure means fluid moved, and the nitrate leads.

And know when not to give a nitrate: hypotension, a recent phosphodiesterase five inhibitor, a right ventricular infarct, and severe aortic stenosis.

One odd stem to recognise. Pulmonary oedema after esmolol, given for an amphetamine tachycardia, still needs nitrates and diuretics.

That's offloading. Now the push.

steps.bridge: That ladder assumed an ordinary failing left ventricle. Some hearts break its rules: a valve, a hole, a rhythm.

lesson.text:
Offloading is done, or the pressure is too low to allow it. Now you push the pump, and this card is the decision tree. Nine bank questions. One entry, one branch, one ending.

The entry is a low pressure with proof of a weak pump: a mean arterial pressure below sixty-five, with an ejection fraction below forty percent or a cardiac index below one point eight.

The branch is one question. Is the right ventricle failing, or is the pulmonary vascular resistance high?

If no, begin dobutamine. If the mean pressure stays below sixty-five, add norepinephrine, and then vasopressin.

If yes, begin milrinone or levosimendan, with norepinephrine from the start. If the mean pressure stays below sixty-five, add vasopressin.

Why those drugs for the right side? Milrinone and levosimendan dilate the pulmonary vessels, and the pulmonary resistance is the afterload of the right ventricle. So they unload it while they strengthen it. But they dilate the systemic vessels too, which is why norepinephrine starts alongside. And vasopressin raises the SVR with a neutral effect on pulmonary resistance.

Both arms end in the same place. If vasopressin fails, consider a mechanical support device.

{{**Entry:** MAP <65 AND (LVEF <40% or CI <1.8)
**RV dysfunction or high PVR?**
**No:** dobutamine → + norepinephrine → + vasopressin
**Yes:** milrinone or levosimendan WITH norepinephrine → + vasopressin
**Both:** then consider a device}}

[[Dobutamine for the failing left ventricle. Milrinone or levosimendan with norepinephrine when the right ventricle or the pulmonary resistance is the problem. Norepinephrine whenever the mean pressure stays below sixty-five.]]

Now the traps. Two bank keys here are out of date.

A pressure of eighty over fifty after fluids: which drug improves the output? One bank keys dopamine. You know from SOAP two why that's outdated. Modern practice is norepinephrine for the pressure and dobutamine for the output. Choose dopamine only if it's the sole vasoactive drug offered. Today it survives mainly in the bradycardia algorithm.

Still hypotensive on dobutamine. One key says decrease it. The card says add norepinephrine, and two more stems with a falling pressure on dobutamine key exactly that. The tempting wrong option is a switch to milrinone, which dilates more.

And one from toxicology. A calcium channel blocker overdose, after calcium and high-dose insulin. Choose by the number that has failed. A low cardiac index needs an inotrope. A low SVR needs norepinephrine.

So that's the ladder. Offload, push, and call for a machine when the drugs run out.

open.text:
You now know the pharmacy: which receptor, which messenger, and which of the three numbers each drug pushes on. This section is about order. Faced with Patient A, cold and wet, what do you do first?

The principle is in the title. Offload first, then push. Why that way round? Because of the price. An inotrope makes an injured heart work harder, and it pays in oxygen. Taking load off costs it nothing.

[[Offload first, then push. Lowering preload and afterload raises the output at no cost in oxygen. An inotrope raises it at a price.]]

The cards run in that order: the place, the targets, the bedside algorithm, the offloading tools, and last the inotrope algorithm.

Listen for two traps. The first is the blood pressure in the stem. A systolic of ninety is the line, and ninety-five is on the safe side of it. The second is dopamine. Two bank keys still choose it, and it's no longer the modern answer.

Start with where this patient should be.

spine: Offload first, then push: lowering preload and afterload raises output at no oxygen cost; an inotrope raises it at a price.
ESC profiles: wet + warm → diuretic and vasodilator. Wet + cold: SBP <90 perfusion first, diuretic later; SBP ≥90 vasodilator + diuretic. Dry + cold → fluid.
Positive pressure lowers LV afterload (transmural pressure) and preload. PEEP: RV preload ↓, RV afterload ↑, LV afterload ↓.
Hypertensive pulmonary oedema (SCAPE): fluid is redistributed, not gained. High-dose nitrate + NIV first; furosemide second; no routine morphine.
Inotrope algorithm: MAP <65 with LVEF <40% or CI <1.8. No RV/PVR problem → dobutamine → norepinephrine → vasopressin. RV/PVR → milrinone or levosimendan WITH norepinephrine.
Dopamine is no longer the first choice in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II); it survives for bradycardia and, on the card, AR. Drugs fail → mechanical support.

questions.text: Shock by subtype: valves, holes and rhythms

steps.bridge: That was the muscle, by profile. Now the valves, where one rule in each lesion is reversed.

lesson.text:
You've met this card in the viva package. It gives each profile of shock its drug.

Classic shock is cold and wet, with a low cardiac index and a high SVR. Norepinephrine comes first, and an inotrope once the patient is stable and after revascularisation. But didn't the bedside algorithm put the inotrope first? It did. That was written for acute heart failure. This was written for shock, where the coronary arteries need a pressure before the muscle is asked to work.

Cold and dry: the same, with small fluid boluses. Warm and wet is cardiogenic shock with a low SVR, often with an inflammatory response after the infarct, or after an arrest. Give norepinephrine, and look for sepsis. And normotensive shock, hypoperfused with a systolic above ninety and a high SVR, may reasonably start with an inotrope.

Right ventricular shock is the one to know. That ventricle needs filling, a low afterload, and a systemic pressure high enough to perfuse it. So give fluid boluses, a pressor, inotropes and inhaled pulmonary vasodilators. The pressor to remember is vasopressin, which raises the SVR with a neutral effect on pulmonary resistance.

[[In right ventricular infarction with hypotension, diuretics and nitrates are the trap. They take the preload from a ventricle that depends on it. Give fluid, then norepinephrine or vasopressin.]]

The discriminator: right ventricular shock has clear lungs and a high venous pressure.

steps.bridge: Valves were four. Four more causes remain where standard treatment harms: a hole, an obstruction, a slow rate, a tight sac.

lesson.text:
Four valve lesions, five bank questions. Sort them by what the heart depends on. The two stenoses need pressure and time. The two regurgitant lesions need unloading.

Aortic stenosis. The valve is fixed, so it sets the flow. Dilate the vessels and the pressure falls, but no more blood can cross the valve to restore it. And the thick ventricle depends on the aortic diastolic pressure for its coronary flow. The card calls it afterload-dependent. So hold the squeeze with a drug that adds no rate: phenylephrine or vasopressin. Inotropy may not help if the ejection fraction is preserved, because the muscle isn't the problem.

You've met this ventricle. In Shock One, a patient with aortic stenosis collapsed the moment he went into atrial fibrillation, because that stiff ventricle fills on its atrial kick. Same heart. It needs its pressure, its rhythm and its filling time.

The bank asks it as a low-flow case, three times. An elderly patient in failure, a weak carotid upstroke, a valve area of zero point seven square centimetres, and a low gradient. The low gradient is the trap. It's low because the stroke volume is low.

[[A valve area below one square centimetre with a low gradient is still severe aortic stenosis. It needs urgent valve replacement. Balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge.]]

Aortic regurgitation. The valve leaks in diastole, so the longer diastole lasts, the more falls back. Keep the heart fast. The card gives dopamine and pacing, for the hypotensive patient. Now the stem only one in five answered. An aortic vegetation, severe regurgitation, pulmonary oedema, and a pressure of one hundred and twenty over seventy. The tempting answers are norepinephrine, epinephrine and furosemide. But with a normal pressure this heart needs unloading: nitroprusside, as a bridge to urgent surgery. Two things are forbidden. A balloon pump, which raises the diastolic pressure and drives more blood back. And a beta-blocker, which lengthens diastole.

Mitral stenosis. Blood needs time to cross a narrow valve, so slow the heart, with esmolol or amiodarone. Avoid chronotropes, and keep the atrial contraction. Hold the pressure with phenylephrine or vasopressin.

Mitral regurgitation. Every rise in afterload sends more blood backwards. So lower the afterload, and here the balloon pump earns its place: it reduces the regurgitant fraction. The stem is an inferior infarct, a new systolic murmur, flash pulmonary oedema, and a pressure of ninety over fifty. That's rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle, which has a single blood supply. Norepinephrine would raise the regurgitation, and milrinone would drop the pressure. The answer is the balloon pump, as a bridge to surgery. Fewer than four in ten chose it.

{{**Lesion** | **Depends on** | **Give** | **Avoid**
AS | pressure | phenylephrine, vasopressin | vasodilators
AR | short diastole | fast rate; nitroprusside if BP normal | IABP, β-blocker
MS | long diastole | esmolol, amiodarone; phenylephrine | chronotropes
MR | low afterload | IABP, inotrope | pure pressor}}

[[The balloon pump helps acute mitral regurgitation and is contraindicated in aortic regurgitation. Raise the heart rate in aortic regurgitation. Slow it in mitral stenosis.]]

steps.bridge: Those are the exceptions. For most patients in cardiogenic shock the cause is simpler: a blocked coronary artery.

lesson.text:
Four more causes where habit does harm. You met this card beside tamponade in the viva package.

A ventricular septal defect after an infarct. The left ventricle now has two exits, the aorta and the hole. Lower the systemic afterload, and more blood goes forwards and less across the septum. So the balloon pump reduces the shunt, as a bridge to surgical or percutaneous closure.

Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. This is the one place in the packet where an inotrope is contraindicated. A small, vigorous ventricle draws the mitral leaflet into its own outflow. So anything that makes the ventricle bigger, slower and gentler relieves it. The stem is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy with hypotension and outflow obstruction, and the best vasopressor is phenylephrine.

[[Dynamic outflow tract obstruction is the exception to the whole ladder. Fill it, constrict it with phenylephrine, slow it, and never give an inotrope or a vasodilator.]]

On echo it's told from pump failure by a small, hyperdynamic ventricle that worsens on dobutamine.

Bradycardia. Treat the cause, and support the rate with pacing or a chronotrope: atropine, isoprenaline, dopamine, dobutamine or adrenaline.

And tamponade, which you know from Shock One by its equal diastolic pressures. Fluid and norepinephrine only buy time. The treatment is drainage.

open.text:
You have a ladder now. Offload, then push, then a machine. It was built for one kind of heart: a left ventricle whose muscle has failed.

This section is about the hearts that break it. A narrow valve. A leaking valve. A hole in the septum. An outflow tract that closes when the ventricle squeezes harder. In each, one rule of the ladder is reversed, and a drug that helped Patient A will harm.

So don't learn tables. Ask one question of each lesion. What does this heart depend on? Pressure, time, or unloading?

[[Stenoses need pressure and time. Regurgitation needs unloading. And every valve in shock needs the valve fixed.]]

The traps here are the most punishing in the packet. Listen for the pressor given to a leaking valve, the balloon pump behind a leaking aortic valve, and the inotrope given to an obstructed outflow.

Begin with the muscle itself, sorted by profile.

spine: Ask what this heart depends on: pressure, time or unloading. The standard ladder can harm a valve, a hole or an obstructed outflow.
Classic cold + wet: norepinephrine first, inotrope once stable and after revascularisation. RV shock: fluid, low PVR, vasopressin (SVR ↑, PVR neutral); no nitrates or diuretics.
Stenoses need pressure and time: AS → phenylephrine or vasopressin, urgent valve replacement; MS → slow the rate (esmolol, amiodarone).
Regurgitation needs unloading: acute AR with normal BP → nitroprusside, never IABP, never slow the rate; acute MR (papillary rupture) → IABP bridge to surgery.
Post-infarct VSD: IABP lowers the shunt. Dynamic LVOT obstruction: fill, phenylephrine, slow; NO inotropes, NO vasodilators.
Tamponade: fluid and norepinephrine only buy time; drain it.

questions.text: Open the artery: revascularisation and the trials

steps.bridge: Open the culprit artery. That rests on one trial, which missed its own primary end point.

lesson.text:
Why does one infarct cause shock when another doesn't? Look at the anatomy. Among patients with infarct shock, fifteen percent have a left main lesion and more than half have triple-vessel disease. So when the culprit closes, the other vessels can't cover for it.

The culprit vessel sets the risk. Left main, a mortality of seventy-eight point six percent. A saphenous vein graft, sixty-nine point seven. The circumflex and the left anterior descending are in effect equal, at about forty-two. The right coronary is lowest, at thirty-seven point four. The logic is how much left ventricle each one feeds.

{{**Culprit vessel** | **Mortality**
Left main | 78.6%
Saphenous vein graft | 69.7%
Circumflex | 42.4%
LAD | 42.3%
RCA | 37.4%
15% have left main disease; >50% triple-vessel}}

You don't need the decimals. You need the order: left main worst, vein graft second, right coronary best.

The card sets revascularisation among the other parts of stabilisation: fluids, oxygenation and ventilation, and antithrombotic drugs. The default is primary angioplasty. Rarely it's bypass surgery, or even emergency transplantation. Fibrinolysis is for when angioplasty can't be done in time.

Two stems. A large anterior infarct, a pressure of seventy-two over forty, a rising lactate: what most improves survival? Early coronary reperfusion. Not high-dose dopamine, epinephrine or a balloon pump.

And the harder one. A raised troponin, recurrent ventricular tachycardia, and an ejection fraction of twelve percent in both ventricles. The tempting answer is an assist device. But a device fixes nothing. Barely a third chose the key.

[[When a shocked heart is probably ischaemic, urgent angiography with a view to revascularisation comes before any device.]]

steps.bridge: Early revascularisation is settled. On the table, the next question: the culprit alone, or every lesion?

lesson.text:
The SHOCK trial of nineteen ninety-nine is why infarct shock goes to the cath lab. It gave Shock One its definition. Here is its result.

Three hundred and two patients with an infarct and cardiogenic shock, randomised to early revascularisation or to medical stabilisation. At thirty days, the primary end point, mortality was similar. Stop there and you'd call the trial negative. That's the trap.

[[SHOCK: no significant difference at thirty days, but a significant fall in mortality with early revascularisation at six months, fifty point three against sixty-three point one percent, and the benefit held at one year.]]

One more line shows what the benefit depends on. With successful angioplasty the mortality was about thirty-five percent. With unsuccessful, about eighty. Your card rounds those; the original paper gives thirty-eight and seventy-nine percent at thirty days. Either way, what decides survival is an open artery.

steps.bridge: Culprit only. One question left from the old habit: does a balloon pump help while you do it?

lesson.text:
The artery is open. But most of these patients have other narrowings. Do you fix them all now?

For years the practice was yes. CULPRIT-SHOCK, in twenty seventeen, tested it in seven hundred and six patients with infarct shock and an identifiable culprit. The end point was death or renal failure needing dialysis at thirty days. Culprit-only angioplasty won, with an absolute risk reduction of nine point five percent. That contradicted widespread practice.

So where did the belief in complete revascularisation come from? From patients who weren't in shock. Three trial names carry it: PRAMI, CvLPRIT and DANAMI three PRIMULTI.

[[In cardiogenic shock, open the culprit artery only. Complete revascularisation is for the stable infarct patient.]]

One discriminator. SHOCK asked whether to revascularise early. CULPRIT-SHOCK asked how much.

steps.bridge: The balloon lost its routine place. To see what it can still do, and what replaced it, look at each machine in turn.

lesson.text:
One more trial, and it's the hinge into the machines. For decades the reflex in infarct shock was a balloon pump. You heard this trial in your viva package.

IABP-SHOCK two, twenty twelve. Six hundred patients with infarct shock, a balloon pump or none. Mortality at thirty days was thirty-nine point seven percent against forty-one point three. No difference, then or at one year or at six.

[[IABP-SHOCK two: no difference in thirty-day mortality with or without the balloon pump. Routine use is class three. Its limitation is that only mild to moderate shock was studied.]]

The balloon keeps a place for the mechanical complications of an infarct, the ruptured papillary muscle and the septal defect.

Now the question actually asked. The trial produced a risk score of six variables, and the stem says all except. Age above seventy-three. A prior stroke. Glucose above one hundred and ninety-one. Creatinine above one point five. Flow below TIMI three after angioplasty. Lactate above five. The planted distractor is a prior myocardial infarction. It isn't in the score. A prior stroke is.

{{**IABP-SHOCK II risk score**
Age >73 years
Prior **stroke** (not prior MI)
Glucose >191 mg/dL
Creatinine >1.5 mg/dL
TIMI flow <3 after PCI
Lactate >5 mmol/L}}

So the balloon lost its routine place. To see why, look at what each machine does to the ventricle.

open.text:
Every drug so far has pushed on a number. None has touched the cause. And the commonest cause of cardiogenic shock is an infarct: a coronary artery has closed, and a large part of the left ventricle has stopped contracting.

So this section asks what actually saves this patient's life. The answer is short. Open the artery.

[[In infarct shock, early reperfusion is the treatment with the strongest proof that it saves lives. Drugs and devices are support.]]

Four cards. First the anatomy. Then three trials, each answering one question. Should you revascularise early? That's SHOCK. Do you open only the blocked artery, or every narrowing? That's CULPRIT-SHOCK. Does a balloon pump help meanwhile? That's IABP-SHOCK two.

The trap is that the names sound alike, and the banks swap them. And one of these trials missed its primary end point, yet changed practice.

Begin with the artery.

spine: In infarct shock early reperfusion has the strongest survival evidence; drugs and devices keep the patient alive until the artery is open.
Anatomy: 15% left main, >50% triple-vessel. Culprit mortality: left main 78.6% > vein graft 69.7% > circumflex 42.4% ≈ LAD 42.3% > RCA 37.4%.
SHOCK (1999, n 302): 30-day mortality similar (46.7% vs 56.0%); 6 months 50.3% vs 63.1%, significant; benefit held at 1 year. An open artery decides survival.
CULPRIT-SHOCK (2017, n 706): culprit-only PCI cut 30-day death or dialysis by 9.5%. Complete revascularisation is for stable patients (PRAMI, CvLPRIT, DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI).
IABP-SHOCK II (2012, n 600): 39.7% vs 41.3%, no difference at 30 days, 1 year or 6 years. Routine IABP class III; score has prior stroke, not prior MI.

questions.text: Devices I: the balloon and the pumps

steps.bridge: Three loops, three machines. Start with the one that nudges the loop least, and is asked the most: the balloon.

lesson.text:
This card is a sketch of three pressure-volume loops. It hasn't been asked, so derive each from where the machine puts the blood.

The balloon deflates as the ventricle ejects, so the ventricle meets a lower pressure. The loop sits slightly lower and wider. The change is small.

An Impella or a TandemHeart takes blood out of the left heart. The ventricle holds less, so the loop shrinks and moves left. That's unloading.

Peripheral VA-ECMO returns blood into the aorta, backwards towards the heart. The aortic pressure rises, a weak ventricle ejects less, and it stays full. The loop moves right and up, and narrows. That's loading. The dashed line, arterial elastance, is the afterload drawn as a slope, and it steepens.

[[The balloon pump nudges the loop lower and wider. A percutaneous assist device shrinks it and shifts it left. Peripheral VA-ECMO shifts it right and up.]]

steps.bridge: The balloon assists a heart that still pumps. The next machine does the pumping itself, from inside the ventricle.

lesson.text:
The balloon pump has lost its routine place, but not its place in the exam. Three grand test questions came from this card.

The word is counterpulsation: the balloon does the opposite of the heart. It holds thirty to fifty millilitres of helium and lies in the descending aorta, its tip just beyond the left subclavian artery and its lower end above the renal arteries.

In diastole it inflates, as the aortic valve closes, at the dicrotic notch. It displaces blood and raises the aortic diastolic pressure. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, so coronary flow improves. That's supply.

In systole it deflates rapidly, just before the valve opens, leaving a space. The ventricle ejects against a lower pressure, so the afterload falls and the stroke volume rises. That's demand. So this push lowers the oxygen bill. It's just small, about half a litre a minute.

[[The balloon inflates in diastole to raise coronary flow, and deflates just before systole to lower left ventricular afterload. It is synchronised with the ECG.]]

Take that last line seriously, because one of your grand test misses hangs on it. The console must know where diastole is. It triggers from the R wave or from the arterial waveform, so it times well only on a regular rhythm. In fast atrial fibrillation the intervals keep changing, the timing slips, and the support fades. So when a stem gives refractory shock with rapid atrial fibrillation and asks which device needs no cardiac synchrony, it's asking you to leave the balloon. The key was Impella. You'll hear the full answer at the end of the packet.

The practical facts. A femoral sheath of seven to eight French. A femoral artery at least four millimetres wide, or the leg becomes ischaemic. Support for days; beyond one to two weeks, limb ischaemia, infection and low platelets rise. NEET's favourite wrong option is a sheath of thirteen to fourteen French, which is the size for an Impella or ECMO.

The contraindications follow from the mechanism: aortic regurgitation of moderate or greater severity, because inflation in diastole drives blood back into the ventricle, then aortic dissection, and severe aorto-iliac disease. The trap is severe left ventricular dysfunction or coronary disease offered as contraindications. Those are indications.

Timing errors. Inflate too early, before the valve closes, and the balloon fills against an ejecting ventricle, so its work rises. Deflate too late, and the balloon is still up when the next ejection begins. That's the most harmful.

{{**Timing error** | **Effect**
Early inflation | LV ejects against the balloon: afterload and LV work ↑
Late inflation | diastolic augmentation lost
Early deflation | augmentation lost; no afterload benefit
Late deflation | most harmful: LV ejects against an inflated balloon}}

And one emergency. Blood in the gas line means the balloon has ruptured. Stop pumping, clamp the line, and remove it at once. A still balloon also collects clot, so it's never left switched off inside the patient.

steps.bridge: A pump across the aortic valve. From that one position come its effects, its contraindications and its signature harm.

lesson.text:
{{**Model:** parasternal long axis, a poorly contracting LV. Highlighted: the LV cavity, the outflow tract and the aortic root. The Impella lies along that line: inlet in the LV, outlet in the root. The model shows the heart, not the catheter.}}

The Impella doesn't assist the pump. It is a pump. Ask the three questions.

Where does it take blood from? The left ventricle. It's a catheter carrying a tiny axial pump, lying across the aortic valve with its tip in the ventricle. In the long axis view from Shock One, picture it along the outflow tract, inlet in the cavity, outlet just above the valve.

Where does it return blood? Into the ascending aorta, flowing forwards, as the heart's own does. So it empties the ventricle.

Your card's numbers, a nine French catheter and a peak flow of four point three litres a minute, belong to the Impella CP. And here's the trap. The shaft is nine French, but the pump head is fourteen, so the sheath is fourteen.

[[The Impella is an axial pump across the aortic valve. It draws blood from the left ventricle and delivers it forwards into the ascending aorta.]]

steps.bridge: Impella empties the LV directly. A second pump empties it from one chamber upstream, and needs a needle through the septum.

lesson.text:
Three consequences of sitting across the aortic valve, and two have been asked.

First, the effect. The cardiac output rises significantly, whether or not the ventricle ejects. And because the pump drains the cavity, the end-diastolic pressure, the wall stress and the myocardial oxygen consumption all fall. More output for less oxygen, where the inotrope gave more output for more. That's unloading.

It's also the one device with a trial in its favour. In DanGer Shock, in twenty twenty-four, the Impella CP lowered mortality at one hundred and eighty days in ST elevation infarct shock, from fifty-eight point five percent to forty-five point eight, at the price of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement. So the American guideline of twenty twenty-five calls it reasonable in selected patients.

Second, the contraindication. The catheter must lie across the valve, so a mechanical aortic valve bars it, and so does a very tight aortic stenosis. One grand test gave shock with severe aortic stenosis, and nearly everyone found it. The distractors, post-cardiotomy failure and acute myocarditis, are indications.

Third, the characteristic risk, which most candidates missed. Haemolysis. A rotor at very high speed shears red cells. The stem asks for the unique complication, and offers pseudoaneurysm and septicaemia. Those follow any large femoral sheath. Only haemolysis belongs to the rotor.

[[Impella raises the output while lowering left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, wall stress and oxygen consumption. It can't cross a mechanical or tightly stenosed aortic valve. Its signature complication is haemolysis.]]

steps.bridge: All three machines so far need lungs that work and a right heart that fills. The last machine needs neither.

lesson.text:
The TandemHeart reaches the same end by another route. Three questions again.

Where does it take blood from? The left atrium. A long cannula goes up the femoral vein into the right atrium and is pushed through the atrial septum. So it's the one device that needs a transseptal puncture.

Where does it return blood? Into the femoral artery, from a pump strapped to the patient's leg. The card's word is paracorporeal, beside the body.

The effect? Oxygenated blood goes from the left atrium to the arteries, bypassing the left ventricle. The output rises, and the ventricle's end-diastolic pressure, wall stress, stroke work and oxygen consumption fall.

Now derive the contraindications, which is what the grand test asked. A ventricular septal defect: empty the left side, and the shunt reverses, sending venous blood to the left, so the patient becomes hypoxaemic. Isolated right ventricular failure: the left atrium is filled by the right heart, so there's nothing to drain. Then severe peripheral vascular disease, a left atrial thrombus, and significant aortic regurgitation.

[[TandemHeart drains the left atrium through a transseptal puncture and returns the blood to the femoral artery. It needs a working right heart, an intact ventricular septum and good femoral vessels.]]

The stem asked which is not a contraindication, and the answer was left ventricular failure, the indication.

One discriminator from the next machine. The TandemHeart drains blood the lungs have already oxygenated, so it needs no oxygenator.

open.text:
The drugs have run out. Both arms of the inotrope algorithm ended on the same line: consider a mechanical support device.

Keep the frame you've used all along. A device is a push on the pump. And ask of it what you asked of every drug. What does it cost the heart? An inotrope raised the output and charged for it in oxygen. A good device raises the output and lowers the heart's work. Some do. One does the opposite, and it's the most powerful of them.

[[For every device ask where it takes blood from, where it returns it, and what that does to the load on the left ventricle.]]

Answer those, and you can derive its effects, its contraindications and its complications.

This section takes the balloon and the two percutaneous pumps. The traps are practical: a sheath size borrowed from the wrong device, an indication offered as a contraindication, and a complication of every femoral device offered as the signature of one.

Begin with one picture that holds all the machines.

spine: Ask of every device: where it takes blood from, where it returns it, and what that does to LV load.
PV loops: IABP slightly lower and wider; pLVAD smaller and shifted left; peripheral VA ECMO narrower, higher and shifted right.
IABP: inflates in diastole (coronary flow ↑), deflates before systole (afterload ↓). 7–8 Fr, femoral artery ≥4 mm, needs a regular rhythm. Never in AR or dissection.
Timing: early inflation raises LV work; late deflation is the most harmful. Blood in the gas line = rupture: stop, clamp, remove.
Impella: axial pump across the aortic valve, LV → ascending aorta; 9 Fr catheter, 14 Fr pump; unloads. Bars: mechanical aortic valve, severe AS. Signature: haemolysis.
TandemHeart: LA → femoral artery by transseptal puncture. Bars: VSD (shunt reverses → hypoxaemia), RV failure, PVD, LA thrombus, AR.

questions.text: Devices II: ECMO and the ladder of support

steps.bridge: ECMO comes in two forms. One question separates them: does the heart need support, or only the lung?

lesson.text:
You met this circuit in your viva package, so take it briefly.

Where does it take blood from? The venous system, usually by a femoral cannula reaching the right atrium. Where does it return it? To the femoral artery, after a pump and a membrane oxygenator.

[[VA-ECMO draws venous blood, oxygenates it, and pumps it into the arterial circulation. It is the only device in this packet that supports gas exchange as well as flow.]]

So it suits the arrest, the failure of both ventricles, and the patient who is hypoxaemic as well as shocked.

But don't reach for it by reflex. In ECLS-SHOCK, in twenty twenty-three, early routine VA-ECMO in infarct shock didn't change thirty-day mortality and caused more bleeding. In the American guideline of twenty twenty-five, routine use is class three, like the balloon.

steps.bridge: VA replaces the heart. Yet it's the one machine that makes the left ventricle's work harder. That's the paradox.

lesson.text:
ECMO has two forms, and the names tell you where the blood goes back. Venoarterial returns it to an artery. Venovenous returns it to a vein.

Take venoarterial. Blood leaves a vein and re-enters an artery, so it has gone around both the lungs and the heart. The circuit does the gas exchange and the pumping. Peripherally that's femoral vein to femoral artery, quick at the bedside. Centrally, after cardiac surgery, it's right atrium to aorta. One grand test showed a picture of the cannulas, and the answer was peripheral, femoral vein to femoral artery.

Now venovenous. Blood leaves a vein, is oxygenated, and returns to a vein. It still has to cross the lungs and be pumped by the patient's own heart. So the circuit does gas exchange only. Cannulation is femoral to jugular, or one double-lumen cannula in the right internal jugular.

So the choice is one question. Does the heart need support, or only the lung? Respiratory failure with an adequate output takes venovenous. Add shock, and it becomes venoarterial.

{{ | **VA** | **VV**
Supports | gas exchange + circulation | gas exchange only
Cannulas | femoral vein → femoral artery | femoro-jugular, or dual-lumen jugular
Native heart | bypassed | does all the pumping
For | cardiogenic shock, arrest | isolated respiratory failure}}

Now the question that was set. A patient on venovenous ECMO for ARDS becomes hyperkalaemic and goes into asystole. The tempting answer is urgent conversion to venoarterial. But think what the circuit does. It puts oxygen into venous blood and moves nothing forwards. With the heart stopped, that blood goes nowhere.

[[Venovenous ECMO gives no circulatory support. A cardiac arrest on it is treated with standard ACLS, starting with chest compressions.]]

Two more wrong options sit there. Defibrillating asystole, when shocks are only for shockable rhythms. And withholding compressions because of the cannulas.

steps.bridge: Blood running backwards up the aorta, against the heart. Three complications follow, and NEET asks all three.

lesson.text:
Put the strongest machine beside the Impella, and the paradox is one table.

On flow, ECMO wins: more than five litres a minute, against two and a half to five. It can replace the whole cardiac output.

On the left ventricle, it loses. Remember the loop that moved right and up. The card says it plainly: ECMO fails to unload. Stroke work is increased, oxygen consumption is unchanged or rising, and arterial elastance is increased. The Impella is the mirror image.

{{ | **VA ECMO** | **Impella**
Flow | >5 L/min | 2.5–5 L/min
LV unloading | fails to unload | unloads
Stroke work | increased | much reduced
MVO2 | unchanged or ↑ | reduced
Afterload | +++ | none
Gas exchange | +++ (only device) | none}}

[[The device with the highest flow doesn't best protect the ischaemic heart. VA-ECMO perfuses the body but raises left ventricular afterload and oxygen demand. Impella gives less flow and truly unloads.]]

And on gas exchange ECMO stands alone, as the only device with an oxygenator.

So sooner or later, someone puts both into the same patient.

steps.bridge: You've met every machine and every price. Now set them on one ladder, bottom to top.

lesson.text:
{{**Model:** parasternal long axis, a poorly contracting LV. Highlighted: LV, left atrium and aortic root. On peripheral VA ECMO, picture this ventricle distending and the aortic valve no longer opening.}}

One fact, three complications. The blood from peripheral VA-ECMO runs backwards up the aorta. Follow it.

Start at the top of the stream. Oxygenated ECMO blood travels up from the groin. The heart's own output comes down from the aortic root. The two meet somewhere in the aorta. While the heart barely ejects, the meeting point lies near the heart, and the whole body gets ECMO blood.

Now the heart recovers, but the lungs are still failing. The ventricle ejects more, and what it ejects hasn't been oxygenated. The meeting point is pushed down the aorta. So the coronaries, the brain and the right arm get dark blood from the heart, while the lower body gets bright blood from the circuit. That's differential hypoxaemia, the Harlequin or north-south syndrome.

Where do you look? The right hand, because its artery comes from the first branch of the arch. The stem gives a saturation of eighty-four percent on the right hand and ninety-nine on the left foot.

The fix? Three tempting options, all wrong. Raise the oxygen on the circuit: that blood is already saturated. Raise the pump flow: that pushes harder against the ventricle. Convert to venovenous: the patient still needs the flow. The answer is to add a return cannula in the internal jugular vein. Oxygenated blood then enters the right heart, crosses the failing lungs, and is ejected already oxygenated. That's VAV.

[[Harlequin syndrome: the right hand is hypoxaemic while the foot is well oxygenated. Monitor the right hand. The fix is a venous return cannula, converting to VAV.]]

Second, stay at the heart. That backwards stream is afterload. A ventricle that can't eject against it still fills, so it distends. The aortic valve stops opening, the arterial trace goes flat, the pulmonary pressures rise, and the lungs flood. On the long axis view you'd see a swollen, still ventricle behind a closed valve. Vent it, with a balloon pump, an Impella or an atrial septostomy. An Impella added to ECMO is called ECPELLA.

Third, the groin. The arterial cannula fills most of the femoral artery, so the leg beyond it starves. Prevent it with a distal perfusion cannula. And if the foot turns cold and pulseless, the answer is an antegrade perfusion cannula at once, not heparin, elevation or thrombectomy.

[[Peripheral VA-ECMO runs blood backwards up the aorta. So put a sensor on the right hand, a vent on the left ventricle, and a perfusion cannula into the leg.]]

Now put the machines on one ladder, from the least support to the most.

The bottom rung is the balloon pump. Counterpulsation, adding roughly half a litre a minute. It modestly lowers the afterload, but it needs a native rhythm and some native output.

The middle rung is the Impella. A microaxial pump from left ventricle to aorta, adding two and a half to five litres a minute. It directly unloads the ventricle, and it's the only one of the three for which that's the primary action.

The top rung is VA-ECMO. Full support of heart and lungs, four to six litres a minute or more. And it increases left ventricular afterload and may need a vent.

{{**Device** | **Flow added** | **LV load** | **Needs rhythm?**
IABP | ~0.5 L/min | afterload slightly ↓ | **yes**
Impella | 2.5–5 L/min | **unloads** | no
VA ECMO | 4–6+ L/min | afterload **↑** | no}}

[[Flow rises from the balloon pump to Impella to VA-ECMO. Only Impella unloads the ventricle as its main action. ECMO gives the most flow and the least unloading.]]

That trade-off is why an Impella is sometimes added to ECMO: one machine for the flow, the other for the ventricle.

Now the question you missed. Refractory shock with rapid atrial fibrillation: which device needs no cardiac synchrony? The key was Impella CP. Here's the honest version. The Impella, the TandemHeart and VA-ECMO are all continuous pumps. None times itself to the heartbeat, and ECMO will support a patient in ventricular fibrillation. Only the balloon needs the rhythm. So the question is really asking you to rule the balloon out.

[[Only the balloon pump needs a regular native rhythm. Impella, TandemHeart and VA-ECMO all run in atrial fibrillation. If the stem asks which device needs no synchrony, the keyed answer is Impella.]]

The evidence sits on the same ladder. The balloon in IABP-SHOCK two: no benefit. VA-ECMO in ECLS-SHOCK: no benefit, more bleeding. Impella in DanGer Shock: lower mortality in selected patients. Of the three, only the machine that unloads has improved survival in a trial.

That returns you to where the packet began. Filling, pump and squeeze. Every drug and every machine pushes on one of them, and the best push without sending the heart a bill for oxygen.

open.text:
Three machines so far, and each supports the left ventricle. Each assumes that the right ventricle can still deliver blood to the left side, and that the lungs can still oxygenate it.

What if neither is true? The cardiac arrest. Both ventricles failing. Shock with hypoxaemia. Then you need a machine that replaces the heart and the lungs at once. That's venoarterial ECMO, at the top of the ladder.

And here is the central paradox of the packet. The machine that gives the most flow does the least for the left ventricle. For the first time, the support itself raises the afterload.

[[VA-ECMO gives the most flow and the least unloading, because its blood runs backwards up the aorta against the left ventricle.]]

Listen for that one fact in every card. Peripheral VA-ECMO returns blood into the femoral artery, and it runs backwards up the aorta. The three complications NEET asks all come from it.

Begin with the circuit.

spine: VA ECMO: venous blood → oxygenator → artery. Supports both ventricles and the lungs; the only device with gas exchange.
VV supports gas exchange only and needs the native heart: arrest on VV ECMO = standard ACLS, compressions at once.
The paradox: most flow (>5 L/min), least unloading. Retrograde aortic flow raises LV afterload, stroke work and MVO2.
Three complications of backwards flow: Harlequin (right hand low, foot high → VAV), LV distension (vent: IABP, Impella, septostomy), limb ischaemia (distal perfusion cannula).
Ladder: IABP ~0.5 L/min < Impella 2.5–5 < VA ECMO 4–6+. Only Impella unloads as its primary action; only the IABP needs a regular rhythm.
Evidence: IABP-SHOCK II and ECLS-SHOCK neutral (routine use class 3); DanGer Shock positive for Impella CP in selected STEMI shock (2a).

close.text:
So let's walk back through it, the way you'll need it in the exam.

You began with Patient A, cold and wet, and one question from Shock One. What do you push with? The answer turned out to be a set of choices, each with a price.

The drugs push through receptors. Beta-one makes the pump stronger and faster. Alpha-one makes the squeeze tighter. And two drugs go around the receptor altogether. The ladder told you the order. Offload a wet heart first, support the pressure next, and push the pump only when the output is truly low. The special cases bent the rules, because a stiff valve or a hole in the septum changes which number you can safely move. Opening the artery is the step that saves lives. And the machines take over when the drugs run out, each one unloading or loading the heart in its own way.

Now the traps. These are the ones you've actually met.

One. A patient on a chronic beta-blocker needs an inotrope. The tempting answer is adrenaline or dobutamine. [[On a chronic beta-blocker, beta-agonists are blunted. Levosimendan or milrinone work beyond the receptor.]] You missed this one twice. Not a third time.

Two. The messengers. [[Beta-one works through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the ryanodine receptor for contraction and phospholamban for relaxation. Alpha-one works through phospholipase C.]] Myosin and its kinases are the wrong answer every time.

Three. A wet patient with a pressure of ninety-five and good perfusion. The tempting answer is a vasopressor. He's wet and warm. He needs a diuretic, and on the flat part of his curve, taking fluid off costs him almost no output.

Four. Shock with disease in several arteries. The tempting answer is to open them all at once. In shock, you open the culprit only. That's CULPRIT-SHOCK.

Five. Venoarterial ECMO gives the most flow, so it must rest the left ventricle. It doesn't. It pumps blood back up the aorta against the ventricle, and the ventricle may distend and need a vent.

And six. A patient in fast atrial fibrillation needs a device. The tempting answer is the balloon pump. The balloon times itself to the heartbeat, so it's the one device that needs a regular rhythm. The pumps and ECMO don't.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each one in your head before you tap it open.

And carry one thought into the next packet. Almost every patient in this packet had an infarct, and almost every trial was about it. So the next packets step back to the start. Before the shock, there's the infarct, and before the infarct, the ECG that shows it. That's where we go next.

drill.q: β1 stimulation speeds relaxation (lusitropy). Which protein is phosphorylated?
drill.a: Phospholamban (by PKA), which frees SERCA2a. Not myosin ATPase (GT7 Q83).

drill.q: Dobutamine raises contractility. Which intracellular step is keyed?
drill.a: Ryanodine receptor phosphorylation (with the L-type Ca²⁺ channel), via Gs → cAMP → PKA. Not myosin kinase inhibition (GT7 Q84).

drill.q: Norepinephrine's α1 effect: which G protein and which enzyme?
drill.a: Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 + DAG. cAMP is the β arm (GT7 Q85).

drill.q: Low output in a patient on a chronic β-blocker: which inotrope?
drill.a: Levosimendan (troponin C sensitiser); milrinone if levosimendan is not offered. Epinephrine and dobutamine are blunted (GT7 Q87, GT8 Q82).

drill.q: Main harm of isoproterenol?
drill.a: Myocardial ischaemia: rate and O₂ demand up, diastolic (coronary perfusion) pressure down.

drill.q: On dobutamine, BP still falling. Next step?
drill.a: Add norepinephrine. Not 'switch to milrinone' (dilates more), not 'reduce dobutamine' unless the stem is about a tachyarrhythmia with adequate BP.

drill.q: Which inotrope accumulates in renal failure, and what do you change?
drill.a: Milrinone (renally excreted): reduce the infusion rate and skip the loading dose.

drill.q: Omecamtiv mecarbil vs serelaxin?
drill.a: Omecamtiv: cardiac myosin activator, more stroke volume without raising cAMP, Ca²⁺ or MVO₂. Serelaxin: relaxin-2 vasodilator, not an inotrope.

drill.q: SOAP II: what differed between dopamine and norepinephrine?
drill.a: 28-day mortality was the same; dopamine gave twice the arrhythmias (24% vs 12%) and more deaths in the cardiogenic subgroup.

drill.q: Septic shock on norepinephrine + vasopressin, now improving. Which is weaned first?
drill.a: Norepinephrine. Stopping vasopressin first causes more hypotension.

drill.q: Septic shock on norepinephrine develops AF with fast rate. Which pressor? And when is vasopressin added?
drill.a: Phenylephrine (pure α1). Vasopressin at norepinephrine 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min.

drill.q: How does methylene blue raise vascular tone? Which 'pressor' on the list is not a drug?
drill.a: Inhibits NO synthase and soluble guanylate cyclase (less cGMP). Angiotensin I is an inactive precursor.

drill.q: Congested, BP 95/60, no hypoperfusion described. Treatment?
drill.a: IV loop diuretic: wet and warm (SBP ≥90). Not norepinephrine.

drill.q: Hypotension appearing after diuresis in a patient who was 120/80?
drill.a: Over-diuresis: stop the diuretic and reassess volume. Not dopamine, not milrinone.

drill.q: Sudden pulmonary oedema, BP 180/100, alert. First line?
drill.a: High-dose IV nitroglycerin + NIV; furosemide second; no routine morphine (NEET 2024, 2025).

drill.q: Haemodynamic effects of PEEP on RV preload, RV afterload and LV afterload?
drill.a: RV preload ↓, RV afterload ↑, LV afterload ↓ (lower LV transmural pressure). NEET 2024.

drill.q: Inotrope algorithm: entry criteria, and the drug for each branch?
drill.a: MAP <65 with LVEF <40% or CI <1.8. No RV/PVR problem: dobutamine → norepinephrine → vasopressin. RV dysfunction or high PVR: milrinone or levosimendan WITH norepinephrine → vasopressin.

drill.q: Acute severe AR, pulmonary oedema, BP 120/70. Drug, and two things to avoid?
drill.a: Nitroprusside as a bridge to surgery. Avoid IABP and β-blockers (only 20% right).

drill.q: Inferior STEMI, new systolic murmur, flash pulmonary oedema, BP 90/50. Diagnosis and bridge?
drill.a: Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture with acute MR. IABP as a bridge to surgery; not norepinephrine or milrinone.

drill.q: Elderly, AVA 0.7 cm², low gradient, in failure. Management?
drill.a: Low-flow low-gradient severe AS: urgent valve replacement (TAVI). Balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge.

drill.q: Takotsubo with LVOT obstruction and hypotension. Best vasopressor, and what to avoid?
drill.a: Phenylephrine, with fluid and rate slowing. Avoid inotropes and vasodilators.

drill.q: SHOCK, CULPRIT-SHOCK, IABP-SHOCK II: one line each.
drill.a: SHOCK: early revascularisation, benefit at 6 months (50.3 vs 63.1%) not 30 days. CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only PCI, 9.5% ARR in death or dialysis. IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality difference (39.7 vs 41.3%).

drill.q: IABP: sheath size, minimum femoral artery, absolute contraindications?
drill.a: 7–8 Fr; artery ≥4 mm. Moderate–severe AR, aortic dissection, severe aorto-iliac disease. (13–14 Fr is Impella/ECMO.)

drill.q: Unique complication of Impella, and its two keyed contraindications?
drill.a: Haemolysis. Mechanical aortic valve and severe aortic stenosis.

drill.q: Femoral VA ECMO: right hand SpO₂ 84%, left foot 99%. Name and fix? And arrest on VV ECMO?
drill.a: Harlequin (differential hypoxaemia): add a jugular venous return cannula (VAV). Arrest on VV: standard ACLS, compressions at once.

traps.trap: β1 improves relaxation by acting on myosin ATPase
traps.truth: PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, releasing SERCA2a, so Ca²⁺ is cleared faster (lusitropy).

traps.trap: Dobutamine raises contractility by inhibiting myosin kinase
traps.truth: PKA phosphorylates the ryanodine receptor and the L-type Ca²⁺ channel. Myosin light chain kinase inhibition is how cAMP relaxes vascular smooth muscle.

traps.trap: Norepinephrine constricts vessels through cAMP
traps.truth: α1 → Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 + DAG. cAMP is the β (Gs) arm.

traps.trap: Epinephrine (or dobutamine) for low output in a patient on a chronic β-blocker
traps.truth: β-agonists are blunted, and epinephrine leaves unopposed α1 vasoconstriction. Levosimendan (keyed) or milrinone works past the receptor.
traps.asked: GT7 Q87 and GT8 Q82 (missed twice)

traps.trap: Isoproterenol's main harm is hypertension or bronchospasm
traps.truth: Myocardial ischaemia: rate and O₂ demand rise while diastolic pressure falls.

traps.trap: On dobutamine, HR 130 and still hypotensive: decrease dobutamine
traps.truth: Disputed DocT key (33% chose it). Reducing dobutamine does not raise pressure: add norepinephrine. Reduce the dose only when the stem is a tachyarrhythmia with adequate BP.
traps.asked: DocT GT, 33% chose the key; 77% right on the tachyarrhythmia version

traps.trap: Tachycardia on dobutamine is a reflex
traps.truth: It is dose-related direct β1 chronotropy, the 'toxic effect'.

traps.trap: Milrinone hypotension is toxicity or bradycardia
traps.truth: It is milrinone-induced vasodilation. It also accumulates in renal failure: lower the rate, no loading dose.

traps.trap: Serelaxin is an inotrope
traps.truth: It is a relaxin-2 vasodilator. Omecamtiv mecarbil is the myosin activator (no rise in cAMP, Ca²⁺ or MVO₂).

traps.trap: A raised lactate on epinephrine means worsening hypoperfusion
traps.truth: Epinephrine raises lactate through β2-driven glycolysis; it can mislead.

traps.trap: SOAP II showed norepinephrine improves overall survival over dopamine
traps.truth: 28-day mortality was the same; dopamine doubled arrhythmias (24% vs 12%) and had more deaths only in the cardiogenic subgroup.

traps.trap: In septic shock with cardiac dysfunction, avoid dobutamine
traps.truth: That is the false statement: add dobutamine to norepinephrine (or epinephrine alone). Dopamine is only for highly selected patients.

traps.trap: Weaning norepinephrine + vasopressin: stop vasopressin first
traps.truth: Taper norepinephrine first; stopping vasopressin first causes more hypotension.

traps.trap: Norepinephrine for septic shock or stroke with AF and fast ventricular rate
traps.truth: Phenylephrine (pure α1) avoids β-stimulation.

traps.trap: Methylene blue raises NO synthase activity or acts on adrenergic receptors
traps.truth: It inhibits NO synthase and soluble guanylate cyclase.

traps.trap: Angiotensin I raises MAP in vasoplegia
traps.truth: It is an inactive precursor needing pulmonary ACE; angiotensin II is the drug (ATHOS-3).

traps.trap: The AHA recommends the cardiac ICU over the general ICU
traps.truth: ESC prefers the CICU; the AHA does not advocate either.

traps.trap: Diuretics drop the output of the wet failing heart
traps.truth: On the flat part of the Starling curve, lowering preload relieves congestion with little loss of stroke volume.

traps.trap: Congestion with SBP 95/60: start norepinephrine
traps.truth: 95 is above 90 and perfusion is intact: wet and warm, IV furosemide.

traps.trap: HFrEF, BP 85/50, HR 120: norepinephrine (or dobutamine) without reading the stem
traps.truth: DocT keys dobutamine (ESC algorithm, 58%); AHA/SCAI start norepinephrine. Low output asking for an inotrope → dobutamine; shock with MAP <65 and norepinephrine offered → norepinephrine.

traps.trap: Hypotension after diuresis: dopamine
traps.truth: Outdated DocT key (42% chose it). Over-diuresis: hold the diuretic, reassess volume; norepinephrine if a drug is needed. Milrinone would vasodilate further.

traps.trap: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema: nitroprusside or morphine as first-line preload reducer
traps.truth: Nitroglycerin. Nitroprusside is kept for refractory hypertension or acute valve regurgitation; morphine is no longer routine.

traps.trap: Renal denervation for recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with resistant hypertension
traps.truth: Pickering syndrome (bilateral renal artery stenosis): renal angiography and stenting.

traps.trap: CPAP mainly reduces preload
traps.truth: Keyed false: it lowers LV afterload as well, by raising intrathoracic pressure and lowering LV transmural pressure (not via alveolar pressure or RAAS).
